item.title: Neutrality in the Constitution: on September 27 the federal vote
item.description: Initiative filed in April 2024 with over 132,000 valid signatures. EU sanctions and military cooperation in the sights of the promoters.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Federal vote on September 27: vote on the neutrality initiative - Filed in April 2024 with over 132,000 valid signatures - The text calls for the shielding of neutrality in the Federal Constitution - EU sanctions resumed after the Russian aggression on Ukraine would become difficult
## Key facts - **What**: Popular initiative to include a comprehensive definition of neutrality in the Federal Constitution - When: Federal vote on September 27; filing of signatures April 2024 - Where: Switzerland, first item on the federal voting agenda - Who: Promoters of the initiative; Federal Council and Federal Chambers (against) - Signatures collected: over 132,000 valid signatures - UN context: Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002 - Exception provided: sanctions ordered by the United Nations would remain allowed - Military cooperation: possible only in the event of aggression or preparatory acts against Switzerland
On September 27, the Swiss electoral body will be called upon to express itself on a foreign policy issue that touches on one of the historical cornerstones of the Confederation: neutrality. The popular initiative, filed in April 2024 with over 132,000 valid signatures collected in support, is the first item on the federal voting agenda.
Neutrality is a principle consolidated over centuries and enshrined in the nineteenth century first by international law and then by the Federal Constitution. It has a permanent nature and ### What would change in practice
The promoters of the initiative judge the resumption of EU sanctions against Russia as a violation of the duty of neutrality and fear a rapprochement with the EU and NATO, with possible drifts towards military dependencies and conflicts. In the field of sanctions, the activists argue that these rarely affect those directly responsible for conflicts, while the effects are often suffered by civilian populations, between deprivation and reduction to hunger. Switzerland, consistent with its humanitarian vocation, should therefore not adhere to coercive measures that burden the innocent. Supporters underline the turbulence of the current international framework and the value of a proven neutrality for conflict prevention and the promotion of peace.
The Federal Council and the Chambers, which voted against the initiative with clear majorities, defend the current margin of manoeuvre in terms of neutrality and recall how it is in any case delimited by international and domestic law. The rigid definition provided for by the text would result in a restriction of the options available to the Confederation.
Opponents point out that the initiative makes demands that, in several respects, are already reflected in the practice followed by the Confederation: what makes the difference, however, are the restrictions provided for in the field of sanctions and cooperation. The federal vote on 27 September requires informed preparation on the part of voters. Here is a concrete three-step procedure.
**1. Read the exact wording.** The text of the initiative is published on the website of the Federal Chancellery, together with the Federal Council's message and the opinions of the parliamentary chambers. Reading the full text is the first step to understanding what would change in the Constitution and which articles would be amended or added.
2. Compare the positions. Supporters and opponents publish their arguments on dedicated websites and in the booklets distributed to voters. The recommendations of parties and of business and trade union associations also help frame the issue. For those living in a bilingual canton or near the border, the positions taken by regional business organisations can offer a local perspective.
3. Check the voting procedure. Voting methods vary by canton and commune: postal voting, in-person voting, or electronic voting where available. It is advisable to check the deadlines for sending in the voting material and, in the case of voting from abroad, the rules provided for Swiss citizens abroad registered with the commune of last residence.
### Where to find support and tools
For those trying to understand the impact of a hardening of neutrality on the Swiss economy, it may be useful to look more closely at the role of good offices and Swiss mediation, historic functions that depend precisely on the flexibility of foreign policy. Those who wish to simulate personal economic scenarios in relation to possible regulatory changes can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to assess the weight of salary deductions and federal taxes, which differ by canton. To compare the cost of living between cantons — also useful for those wondering where economic neutrality weighs most — the dedicated page on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) is available.
### After the vote: what to expect
Regardless of the outcome, the practical consequences will not be immediate: the entry into force of any constitutional amendment follows the timeframes set by federal law. For citizens and businesses, the most effective way to stay up to date remains monitoring the official communications of the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellery, which will publish the regulatory developments linked to the popular decision. For those seeking operational support in managing their personal finances in CHF, the [payslip tool](nav:payslip) and the [calculator](nav:calculator) remain reliable starting points to find their bearings.

item.title: Opening a business in Obvaldo: trade register and costs
item.description: Practical guide to legal form, registration in the commercial register, minimum capital and charges for starting a business in the Canton of Obvaldo.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Legal form: choice between joint-stock company, legal entity or sole proprietorship - Minimum capital: CHF 20,000 (Sagl) or CHF100,000 (Sa) - Registration in the trade register mandatory for corporate forms - Variable registration fees at cantonal and federal level
## Key facts - **What**: Procedure to open a business in Canton Obvaldo - Where: Canton Obvaldo, central Switzerland - Who: Cantonal Authority and Trade Register Office - Taxes: 3 levels (federal + cantonal + municipal DFI) - Minimum capital: To be verified according to the legal form - Social contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - Insurance obligation: LAMal mandatory within 3 months of arrival
Starting a business in Canton Obvaldo means moving within a uniform Swiss regulatory framework in substance, but with specific cantonal declinations with regard to taxes, registration fees and administrative charges. The first concrete decision concerns the legal form, because this choice results in minimum capital, accounting obligations, responsibilities and recurring costs.
The main options for those who intend to operate in Obvaldo as an entrepreneur are the sole proprietorship, the joint venture, the limited partnership, Sagl (a limited company) and Sa (a limited company). The first three are not subject to registration in the commercial register, while Sagl and Sa must Choosing the legal form is not just a tax issue: it determines the level of personal responsibility, the ability to raise capital and the accounting obligations. A sole proprietorship is suitable for a low-risk and low-volume business; Sagl and Sa instead offer liability limited to the capital contributed and a structure more suitable for growth and investment.
### Practical implications of salary contributions
Those who start a business and intend to hire staff must consider mandatory social security and insurance contributions in Switzerland. The following apply to the salary paid: AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% borne by the employee, 10.6% total with the employer's share), AD/AC (1.1% up to the annual ceiling provided), LAINF/LAA with rates between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity, and contributions to the second pillar (LPP/BVG) calculated on the salary coordinated according to the age group: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55 years up to the reference age). The AVS reference age is currently 65 for men and 64 for women, under harmonisation.
For the owner himself, who is often initially also an employee of his company, the same logic applies: the salary must be consistent with the AVS compensation funds and registered with the compulsory occupational pension fund once the threshold for access to the LPP has been exceeded.
### Insurance and health obligations
Health insurance ### Procedura step-by-step per aprire un'attività in Obvaldo
Passo 1 — Scegliere la forma giuridica. Per attività a basso rischio e con un solo titolare conviene spesso la ditta individuale, che evita l'iscrizione al registro di commercio. Per attività che puntano a crescita, investimenti o responsabilità limitata, Sagl (capitale minimo CHF 20'000) o Sa (CHF 100'000) sono le opzioni standard.
Passo 2 — Verificare la disponibilità della ragione sociale. Prima di costituire la società è opportuno verificare che il nome desiderato non sia già registrato nel registro di commercio svizzero (consultabile online a livello federale).
Passo 3 — Aprire un conto bancario vincolato. Per Sagl e Sa è necessario aprire un conto di deposito del capitale presso una banca svizzera; la banca rilascia una conferma di versamento che andrà allegata alla domanda di iscrizione.
Passo 4 — Redigere l'atto di costituzione e lo statuto. Per Sa e Sagl l'atto costitutivo è un atto pubblico, che in Svizzera richiede la forma autentica davanti a un notaio. Lo statuto disciplina oggetto sociale, capitale, organi e diritti dei soci.
Passo 5 — Iscrivere la società al registro di commercio. La domanda di iscrizione viene presentata all'ufficio cantonale del registro di commercio in Obvaldo, con tutti gli allegati richiesti (atto costitutivo, statuto, conferma bancaria, identità dei fondatori e degli organi).
Passo 6 — Registrarsi presso le autorità fiscali. Dopo l'iscrizione al registro, la nuova entità viene comunicata all'amministrazione cantonale delle contribuzioni, che assegna il numero di contribuente e indica gli obblighi dichiarativi per IFD, imposta cantonale e comunale. Se prevista attività con volume d'affari superiore alla soglia IVA, va effettuata l'iscrizione presso l'AFC/ESTV per l'imposta sul valore aggiunto.
Passo 7 — Iscriversi alle assicurazioni sociali. Il datore di lavoro (anche il titolare che versa uno stipendio a sé stesso) deve affiliarsi a una cassa di compensazione AVS e, se del caso, a una cassa pensioni LPP. La SUVA gestisce l'assicurazione infortuni obbligatoria per i dipendenti; per il titolare indipendente l'adesione è facoltativa ma consigliata.
Passo 8 — Stipulare la LAMal. Il titolare e ogni persona residente in Svizzera deve stipulare un'assicurazione malattia obbligatoria entro tre mesi dall'arrivo o dal trasferimento del domicilio. La scelta della franchigia (CHF 300–2'500 per gli adulti) incide direttamente sul premio mensile.
### Scadenze e adempimenti successivi
Una volta avviata l'attività, vanno rispettate le scadenze periodiche: dichiarazione delle imposte (modulo cantonale e modulo federale), versamenti IVA (di norma trimestrali secondo il metodo concordato con l'AFC), contributi AVS/AI/IPG/AD mensili o trimestrali, premio LAINF e premio LPP. Le quattro date di voto federali all'anno possono occasionalmente riguardare anche temi economici rilevanti per le imprese (riforme fiscali, AVS, LPP); in tali occasioni le conseguenze di un sì o di un no vanno valutate caso per caso.
Per supporto concreto nel calcolo dello stipendio e dei contributi che gravano su dipendenti e datore in Svizzera, è disponibile il [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) di Frontaliere Ticino, utile sia in fase di costituzione sia nella gestione corrente del personale. Per approfondire il confronto dei premi cassa malati tra Cantoni e regioni, è attivo il comparatore casse malati, mentre per la dichiarazione delle imposte e la pianificazione fiscale la [guida dichiarazione imposte](nav:tax-return) offre un quadro operativo aggiornato.

item.title: AVS and complementary services in the Canton of St. Gallen
item.description: How the first pillar works in the Canton of St. Gallen: compensation fund, pension calculation and PC to cover the living minimum.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Canton of St. Gallen Compensation Fund manages AVS contributions and annuities - Supplementary benefits (PC) cover the minimum living allowance of those entitled - Contribution gaps can reduce the AVS income proportionally - LUFAS/BSV coordinates social security at the federal level
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal Clearing House of St. Gallen (Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen) - When: Not yet specified in source - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland - Who: UFAS/BSV (Confederation) + cantonal clearing houses - Amount: Specific data on annuities and PC thresholds not reported in the source - Legal basis: AVS/AHV managed by the first pillar of Swiss social security - Tools: AVS annuity calculator on the official federal website - Reference: UST/BFS publishes statistics on pensions and PC beneficiaries
Swiss social security is divided into three pillars: the first is the AVS/AHV, which is mandatory for anyone who carries out a gainful activity in Switzerland. In the Canton of St. Gallen, as in all the Cantons, the collection of contributions and the payment of AVS annuities are entrusted to the cantonal compensation fund, which operates under the supervision of the UFAS/BSV at the federal level. The compensation fund is the first point of contact for workers, employers and recipients of annuities.
Registration with the compensation fund generally takes place through the employer, who pays the contributions ## Key facts - **What**: Complementary services (PC) as a safety net of the first pillar - When: Entitlement assessed year by year based on income and substance - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, cantonal PC office - Who: Confederation (UFAS/BSV) + Canton for financing - Amount: Specific amounts and substance thresholds not reported in the source - Procedure: Request at the PC office of the Canton of St. Gallen
When the AVS annuity, possibly added to other benefits of the first and second pillar, is not sufficient to cover the minimum living allowance recognized by law, the supplementary benefits (PC) intervene. It is a benefit subject to conditions of income and substance, financed in part by the Confederation and in part by the Cantons. The UFAS/BSV defines the regulatory framework, while the operational management is entrusted to the cantonal offices of the PCs — also in the Canton of St. Gallen.
### Who is entitled to PCs and how they are calculated
Persons who receive an AVS or AI annuity and whose determining income, net of recognized expenses, does not exceed the recognized expenses for vital needs are potentially entitled to PCs. The expenses recognized include an amount for vital needs (distinguished by single, couple, family), actual rental expenses within a maximum, compulsory health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG) up to an average cantonal amount, and additional items for particular situations such as
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Key facts - **What**: Operational procedure for claiming AVS pensions and supplementary benefits - When: Applications at any time, with effect from the date of submission - Where: Compensation fund + PC office of the Canton of St. Gallen - Who: Insured person, employer, cantonal office - Documents: AVS account statement, salary certificates, asset documentation
Obtaining the AVS pension and, if necessary, supplementary benefits is a path that may seem bureaucratic but follows clear steps. Here is how to proceed concretely in the Canton of St. Gallen.
### Step 1: Verify your AVS account
The first step is to request the individual AVS account statement, which lists all recorded earnings and credits for childcare or care tasks. The statement can be obtained online via the federal portal or at the cantonal compensation fund. Any missing income must be reported with supporting documentation (salary certificates, employer attestations).
### Step 2: Apply for the AVS pension
The AVS pension is not paid automatically: it must be formally requested from the compensation fund of the Canton of St. Gallen approximately three to six months before reaching reference age. The application can be submitted online or in paper form and requires personal and bank details as attachments.
### Step 3: Consider redeeming contribution gaps
If the account statement shows contribution gaps in the last five years, a redemption can be considered. However, the redemption is only partly tax-deductible and must be assessed case by case: for people with high incomes, it is often better to leave the gap and compensate through PC; for people with substantial assets, redemption may be more efficient.
### Step 4: Apply for supplementary benefits
If the AVS pension (plus LPP) does not cover the recognised vital needs, a PC application must be submitted to the competent office of the Canton of St. Gallen. Income, asset, rental expense, and LAMal premium documentation are required. The PC is recalculated annually based on the financial situation.
### Step 5: Coordination with other instruments
PC does not exclude other benefits: it cumulates with the reduction of LAMal premiums (cantonal subsidy) and can be supplemented by social assistance benefits for those who still do not reach the minimum subsistence level. It is advisable to also check any entitlement to family supplementary benefits and other cantonal reductions.
To estimate the expected AVS pension amount, the [AVS pension calculator](nav:pension) is useful. To assess the tax impact of a possible redemption, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) provides an initial indication of net income and applicable deductions in the Canton of St. Gallen.

item.title: AVS and PC in the Canton of St. Gallen: the clearing house
item.description: AVS cashier and PC office are two separate entities: this is how the first pillar works in St. Gallen and when to ask for complementary services.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - AVS first pillar: federal income calculated on a national scale with periodic adjustments - Canton of St. Gallen: the cantonal compensation fund manages AVS contributions and annuities - Complementary services: dedicated cantonal office, separate from the AVS fund - Contribution gaps: extend the contribution period with voluntary payments
## Key facts - **What**: AVS Canton of St. Gallen Compensation Fund and Supplementary Benefits Office - Who: Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen for AVS; Kantonsstelle für Ergänzungsleistungen for PCs - Where: Canton of St. Gallen (German-speaking Switzerland) - When: system in place, operational details updated by cantonal authorities - How it works: cash collects AVS contributions and calculates annuities; PCs are managed by a separate office - Amount: annuity and benefits calculated according to federal legislation AHVG/LPC
In the Canton of St. Gallen, the first pillar of Swiss social security is divided into two distinct bodies that residents must know how to recognize to avoid bureaucratic misunderstandings. The cantonal clearing house — Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen — is the entity that collects the AVS/AI/IPG contributions from workers and employers, calculates the AVS annuities and pays the federal benefits of the first pillar. When an insured reaches the reference age and submits the pension application, it is this fund that verifies the years of contribution, the credits for educational tasks ## Practical analysis: AVS income, gaps and vital minimum
The AVS annuity is not a fixed amount, but the result of a calculation that combines the years of contribution, the average of the income subject to contribution, and credits for educational or assistance tasks. If you are applying for an annuity in the canton of St. Gallen, please contact Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen attaching the individual account statement, salary certificates and any document certifying periods of activity abroad or stay. The cashier then transmits the decision with the indication of the monthly income due.
### What happens in case of contribution gaps Contribution gaps — years in which contributions were not paid, perhaps because the person resided abroad without bilateral agreements or exercised non-subject activity — proportionally reduce the income. The law provides for the possibility of covering them by paying arrears or voluntary contributions, but only under certain terms and conditions. A policyholder who discovers a gap in their individual account can ask the compensation fund for a recovery calculation, knowing that the cost increases with age and that the operation is especially convenient at a young age.
### When supplementary services are triggered Complementary benefits come into play when the AVS income, combined with other income (LPP, foreign income, income from substance), does not cover the expenses recognized by the LPC: vital needs,
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## What to do concretely: procedure and deadlines
Obtaining the AHV pension or supplementary benefits in the Canton of St. Gallen requires specific steps and adherence to deadlines. The AHV pension application must be submitted to the Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen approximately six months before reaching the reference age. For supplementary benefits, the application is submitted to the Kantonsstelle für Ergänzungsleistungen, attaching the latest AHV pension decision, the LPP pension fund statement, the tax return, and any documentation regarding assets and debts.
### Operational checklist - Request the individual AHV account statement from the Central Compensation Office in Geneva or from the cantonal fund - Verify the completeness of contribution years and identify any gaps - If there are gaps: ask the Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen for a calculation of voluntary or backdated contributions - Submit the AHV pension application approximately six months before the retirement age - Once the AHV decision is received, assess whether the pension covers the minimum subsistence level - If not, submit an application for supplementary benefits (EL) to the Kantonsstelle für Ergänzungsleistungen - Attach all required income and asset documentation
### Useful tools and deadlines EL decisions are recalculated annually: income and assets must be reported every year, failing which payments are suspended. For those already receiving the AHV pension who notice a change in income or family situation (marriage, widowhood, birth of children), it is advisable to submit a new EL application so that eligibility can be reassessed.
To simulate the AHV pension amount and understand the impact of any contribution gaps, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) is useful, as it allows you to estimate contributions paid over time and the projected pension. item.title: Rentals in the Canton of St. Gallen: lease and market rights
item.description: Uniform rental right throughout Switzerland (CO art. 253 et seq.): maximum deposit of 3 months, dispute of the rent within 30 days.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The CO (art. 253 et seq.) regulates the lease in a uniform manner throughout Switzerland - The security deposit cannot exceed 3 months of rent and goes to a restricted account - The dispute of the initial fee must be submitted within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Cantons and areas affect average canons: St. Gallen is not a single market
## Key facts - **What**: legal framework of the residential lease in the Canton of St. Gallen - When: current federal law (CO art. 253 et seq.), constant application over time - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, with differentiation by areas (urban, peri-urban, rural) - Who: landlord and tenant subject to the Code of Obligations; cantonal conciliation authorities competent for disputes - Amount: maximum security deposit equal to 3 months' rent (not 4, not 6) - Expiry: 30 days to challenge the initial fee before the conciliation authority - Instrument: lease conciliation authority, cantonal body in charge - Principle: same federal lease law in each canton; the variability is on market rents, not on the law
The lease of dwellings and commercial premises is governed by the Code of Obligations (art. 253 et seq.): this is federal law, the same in every Swiss canton. In the Canton of St. Gallen, as in the rest of the Confederation, the relationship between landlord and tenant therefore responds to uniform rules, while what ## St Gallen Rental Market Analysis: What Really Changes for Home Seekers
The Canton of St. Gallen has a heterogeneous rental market: urban and peri-urban areas, in particular the city of St. Gallen and neighboring municipalities, show higher rents than rural and mountain areas. The differential is driven by demand (jobs, university, transport supply) and housing availability, not by different cantonal legislation. Those who move to St. Gallen city or a neighboring municipality must therefore take into account higher fees than those who choose an inner valley or a peripheral municipality.
For a potential tenant, there are three critical steps: the verification of the initial rent with respect to the local market, the constitution of the security deposit and the knowledge of their own protection tools in case of disputes. Let's look at them concretely.
### Step 1 — Check the fee before signing
The initial rent is freely agreed, but must be plausible compared to comparable rentals in the same area. In the absence of official figures published for the Canton of St. Gallen at the level of the individual Municipality, it is useful to consult:
- Comparable listings on real estate portals active in Switzerland (for similar premises, same area, same size); - Aggregate data published by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO/BFS) on the structure of rentals at the national level; - Indications provided by the associations of
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## What to do concretely in Canton St. Gallen: procedure, deadlines and tools
Renting a home in Canton St. Gallen means facing a precise procedure, with strict deadlines that, if ignored, jeopardize the tenant's rights. Here is an operational guide in four steps.
### Step 1 — Before signing: rent verification
Before signing the lease, compare the proposed rent with: - at least 5–10 similar listings in the same area (same square footage, same type of property, same fittings); - statistical data published by the SFSO (FSO) on the structure of rents in Switzerland; - indications from tenants' associations active in Canton St. Gallen.
If the rent appears abnormal, negotiating before signing is the most effective route. After signing, only ex post tools remain available.
### Step 2 — At signing: security deposit and contract
Verify that the requested deposit does not exceed 3 months' rent. Ask that it be set up in a blocked account held in the tenant's name, at a bank or an insurance company. Keep the payment receipt and all contractual documentation (signed lease, house rules, any ancillary agreements).
Carefully read the clauses on duration, notice periods, rent adjustments and the breakdown of ancillary costs. If anything is unclear, request written clarification before signing.
### Step 3 — Within 30 days: possible rent challenge
If the initial rent is deemed excessive, the tenant may file a challenge with the conciliation authority for tenancy matters of Canton St. Gallen within 30 days of taking possession of the dwelling. The procedure is usually free of charge or low-cost for the parties. The authority first attempts mediation; if it fails, it refers the case to the ordinary court.
### Step 4 — Financial difficulties and affordable rent
If the burden of rent on the household budget becomes critical, it is worth checking whether your municipality or canton provides specific support. At the federal level, tenancy law does not provide direct rent subsidies, but complementary tools exist — including reductions in health insurance premiums (LAMal) for low-income households — that can ease the overall cost of living in Switzerland.

item.title: AVS and complementary services in Canton Obvaldo: the guide
item.description: How the first AVS pillar works in the Obvaldo Canton: role of the compensation fund, contribution gaps and complementary benefits to cover the minimum living wage in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - First pillar in Switzerland: AVS income calculated on income and years of contribution - Cantonal Compensation Fund manages contributions and benefits - Contribution gaps may reduce the amount of the AVS annuity - Supplementary benefits cover the minimum living allowance when the annuity is not enough
## Key facts - **What**: AVS/AHV first pillar and complementary services to cover the minimum living - Where: Canton Obvaldo (Obwalden), with reference to the Swiss system - Who: Cantonal Compensation Fund of Obvaldo; Federal Office of Social Insurance UFAS/BSV for federal legislation - Amount: not yet specified in the source for the minimum AVS annuity and supplementary benefits in the Obvaldo Canton - When: system in force in 2026 according to the source - How: calculation of the AVS annuity based on the average of the determining incomes and the years of contribution
The Swiss social security system rests on three pillars, and the first — old-age and survivors' insurance (AVS/AHV) — is managed at the federal level but enforced through cantonal compensation funds. In the Canton of Obvaldo, as in the rest of Switzerland, each resident is required to pay AVS contributions from 1 January following the age of 17, continuing until the reference age. The collection of contributions and the payment of benefits pass from the cantonal compensation fund of Obvaldo, which acts as The practical implications of the first pillar affect all residents in Switzerland, regardless of their canton of domicile. Understanding how the AHV/AVS pension mechanism and supplementary benefits work means knowing what levers each insured person has to avoid reductions or, conversely, to access support when the pension is not enough.
### Concrete implications at the national and cantonal level
The AVS/AI/IPG contribution is deducted from every salary paid in Switzerland, and the principle of the place of work determines to which cantonal fund the contributions are directed. This means that an employee working in the Canton of Obwalden pays their contributions to the Obwalden fund, even if they reside in another canton. The system is uniform at the federal level, but each cantonal fund has its own operational margins in managing accounts, payment timing, and assistance to insured persons. For those who change cantons during their career, the contributions paid remain valid for the purpose of calculating the pension: what matters is the sum of the years and incomes recorded at the federal level, not the canton that collected them.
From a pension standpoint, the first pillar is designed to cover the minimum subsistence level in combination with the LPP/BVG (second pillar) and the third pillar 3a. When this coverage is not achieved — for example, due to careers with modest incomes, periods of inactivity, or contribution gaps — supplementary benefits come into play. Supplementary benefits (PC in Italian, EL in German, PC in French) are not an automatic right: the Obwalden fund assesses the applicant's overall economic situation, taking into account income, assets, and recognized needs.
### Before vs. after: what changes with gap management
Before addressing gaps, the AVS/AVS pension is calculated only on the years actually contributed, with proportional reductions as a result. After the payment of missing contributions or the recognition of equivalent periods (education, caring for family members, etc.), the pension may increase. This is why the individual account is the key tool: the cantonal fund is required to provide a copy upon request, and the insured person can submit their observations. The cost of catch-up contributions is determined by law and must be paid to the fund managing the account.
### Scenario: who may need supplementary benefits
A retiree who has worked for a long time at low wages, with reduced contribution years due to stays abroad or periods of education not credited, may find themselves with a modest AVS pension. If even the LPP/BVG has not generated sufficient retirement assets — for example, because they have always worked below the coordination threshold — total pension coverage may not be sufficient to meet the recognized subsistence needs. In such cases, supplementary benefits come into play as a last-resort instrument, funded by the community, but they require a formal application and the submission of complete asset and income documentation.
At the national level, the system is funded partly by salary contributions and partly by federal funds and VAT, according to a pay-as-you-go mechanism involving the FSIO/UFAS and the Confederation. The Canton of Obwalden participates in operational management through its own compensation fund, under federal supervision. The distinction between those who set the rules (FSIO/UFAS) and those who apply them (cantonal funds) is essential to understanding who to contact: for pension calculation, gap recovery, or supplementary benefit applications, the point of contact is the Obwalden fund, even though the legal basis is federal.
For those who want to orient themselves better, a [dedicated tool for pension and retirement planning](nav:pension) allows simulating the impact of different contribution careers on the estimated pension amount, without replacing the role of the cantonal fund.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). Checking your AVS situation is a concrete action that every resident in Switzerland can take in a few steps. The cantonal compensation office of Obwalden is the operational point of contact for those who work or reside in the canton.
### Step-by-step procedure: how to find your way
1. **Request the individual account (CI)**: the Obwalden compensation office sends the CI periodically, but it can be requested at any time. It is the document showing all registered income and credited years of contributions. 2. Check for any gaps: if years or months are missing, it is possible to ask the office how to fill the gap, for example through recovery contributions or by counting equivalent periods (education, caregiving). 3. Estimate the future pension: upon request, the office provides a projection of the AVS pension based on the registered data. For more detailed simulations, an external pension planning tool is also useful. 4. Plan the 3a pillar: if the projected AVS pension is modest, the 3a pillar allows you to accumulate supplementary capital with a tax advantage. The maximum payable amount is indexed every year. 5. Submit a PC application if needed: when the AVS pension plus other income does not cover the vital needs, it is possible to apply for supplementary benefits to the Obwalden office, attaching the required income and asset documentation.
### Documents typically required
For the request of the individual account, an identity document is sufficient. For the PC application, instead: the statement from the compensation office with the assigned AVS pension, the statements from the LPP/BVG pension fund, the tax certificate, the land registry extract, bank and postal statements, and any other proof of income or assets. The cantonal office provides the updated list and forms.
### Deadlines and timing
There is no single deadline for submitting the PC application: it is submitted when the need arises, normally upon reaching the AVS reference age. However, the application is generally retroactive only for a limited period, so it is advisable to submit it promptly. Payment starts from the month in which the complete application was received by the office.
### Difference between PC and LAMal premium reduction
Supplementary benefits should not be confused with the premium reduction of mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG). The latter is a cantonal subsidy on health insurance premiums, managed by the competent cantonal office, and does not depend on the compensation office. The two benefits can be combined, but they are separate applications. For the healthcare part, you can also consult a [health insurance premium comparison tool](nav:health).
For those who want to estimate the overall impact on the payslip and on the future pension, the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) is the starting point to evaluate the AVS/AI/IPG contribution withheld and compare it with the expected pension.

## In a nutshell - Own funds and mortgage are inseparable components of any Swiss real estate purchase - Swiss taxation operates on 3 levels: federal, cantonal and municipal - Transfer tax is a cantonal/municipal levy that applies at the time of transfer of ownership - Notary fees and registration in the land register complete the cost framework

### The path of real estate purchase in the Canton of St. Gallen
Buying property in the Canton of St. Gallen is an important decision that involves a cascade of financial and administrative factors. It's not just a matter of finding the right property: behind it is a complex structure of assessments, financing and tax levies that follow precise rules.
The first step is to assess your financial capacity. Those who want to buy do not start from scratch: they need their own funds (the initial capital paid at the time of signing) and a mortgage to cover the rest. Swiss banks assess the sustainability of this debt based on the buyer's income, other existing liabilities and the stability of its status ## Three-level taxation and the transfer tax
The Swiss tax system operates on three levels simultaneously: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Anyone buying a house in the Canton of St. Gallen enters directly into this multi-layered system, as the acquisition of real estate triggers tax obligations at both the cantonal and municipal levels. Each level has different competences: federal taxation mainly concerns direct federal tax and VAT, while cantonal and municipal administration handles real estate property taxes, the transfer tax, and municipal fees.
The most relevant element for buyers is the transfer tax (also known as the 'acquisition tax' in some cantons). This is a cantonal and/or municipal levy that applies to the transfer of ownership. Unlike other property taxes, the transfer tax is paid only once at the time of purchase and varies significantly from canton to canton: some cantons have higher rates, others lower; some municipalities within the same canton may apply additional tiers.
### Notary procedures and registration
Before becoming the official owner, the buyer must use the services of a notary, who drafts the deed of sale and manages the payments. The notary verifies that the seller is indeed the owner, that there are no hidden mortgages, and that all costs (including the transfer tax owed to the canton and the municipality) are paid correctly. Notary fees vary based on the value of the property and according to the rates set by the canton.
Once the notarial deed has been drawn up and all funds have been paid, the notary submits the file to the cantonal land registry. This is where the transfer of ownership becomes official: the buyer appears as the new owner in the registry, the mortgage is registered as security for the debt to the bank, and the sale is completed. This process is an integral part of your [pension](nav:pension) planning: a real estate investment reduces the capital to be paid into other retirement instruments.
### Managing total costs
Those buying a house must consider not only the purchase price. In addition to the mortgage and own funds, the calculation includes notary fees (typically a percentage of the property's value), the transfer tax, and potentially a registration fee. The total of these additional costs can reach up to 5-10% of the purchase price, depending on the tax structure of the municipality in the Canton of St. Gallen.
Furthermore, costs do not end with the purchase: every owner will have to pay real estate property taxes (cantonal and municipal property tax), maintenance expenses, and any contributions for condominium improvements. It is therefore important to consider a property purchase not as an occasional expense, but as a decision that affects the family budget for decades.

The Swiss family allowance system is based on a double level: the Federal Law on Family Allowances (LAFam) establishes the common rules valid in all cantons, while each canton - including St. Gallen - regulates amounts, ancillary conditions and competent fund through its own legislation. In the Canton of St. Gallen, allowances are paid by recognized family compensation funds, which operate under the supervision of the responsible cantonal office. For those who work in Switzerland - as an employee or as a self-employed person - coverage is mandatory and follows criteria linked to the family unit, the age composition of the children and, in some cases, the level of income.
### Who is entitled to benefits in St. Gallen
The law provides the right for employees subject to the AVS contribution obligation and for self-employed workers registered with the corresponding funds. The so-called "equal cross-border workers" who carry out gainful employment in Switzerland and pay contributions are also entitled to it, provided that their children fall within the definition of "child" pursuant to the LAFam (own children, spouse's children, foster children, orphans and, within certain limits, cohabiting brothers and sisters). For children in education, the right is extended until they reach the age of 25, provided that they attend school or undertake a recognized internship. The Canton of St. Gallen, through its implementing law, has the task of defining the monthly amounts per child and per child in education, as well as any birth or adoption allowances, remaining within the scope of the federal minimums.
The exact amount of monthly allowances paid in St. Gallen is defined year by year by cantonal legislation and may include differentiations based on the child's age or type of education. For the current value it is necessary to consult the official website of the Canton or the relevant family compensation fund, since the figures are not established in this article. ## Analysis: what changes for families and employers
Compared to the past, the system of family allowances has been progressively standardised by the LAFam, which came into force in 2009. Before that date, each Canton could decide whether or not to establish a family compensation fund. Today, on the other hand, the contributory obligation is extended to all employers and the right to benefit is harmonized at the federal level, without prejudice to the right of the Cantons to provide higher amounts or additional benefits. St. Gallen fits into this logic by offering, like other cantons in German-speaking Switzerland, a structure of family coffers parallel to the AVS coffers, with contributory obligations calculated on the wage bill.
### Practical implications for those living and working in Switzerland
For a family residing in Switzerland with dependent children, the allowance represents a non-taxable monthly income supplement, which is added to the salary and does not affect the calculation of direct federal tax or cantonal and municipal taxes. On the employer's side, payment is normally made through the family compensation fund to which the company is affiliated: contributions are deducted from the wage bill and benefits are paid through the wage circuit. For an independent worker, the fund pays directly to the beneficiary, subject to registration and payment of contributions.

The B residence permit is one of the main Swiss residence documents for foreigners who intend to reside and work in the federal territory. Unlike the C (domicile) permit, the B permit is renewable and is intended for those who have not yet accumulated enough years of residence to access a definitive status. In Canton Obvaldo, as in all Swiss cantons, the cantonal migration office is the authority responsible for the issuance, renewal and administrative management of the B permit.
### Key features of permit B
Permit B represents an intermediate category in the Swiss system of residence permits managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). This document allows the foreigner to live, work and settle in the territory of Switzerland for the duration of the permit. Its renewable nature distinguishes it from the L permit (of short duration, up to 1 year) and makes it a less definitive title than the C permit. The duration of the B permit is not standardized at the federal level, but varies based on cantonal decisions and individual circumstances. Usually, the first renewal or the initial issuance covers a period of 1 to 5 years. The permit is automatically renewable if the underlying conditions (employment, means of subsistence) remain met and there are no grounds for refusal.
### Who can apply for permit B
Permit B is generally open to third-country nationals (outside the EU/EFTA) with a legitimate job offer, EU/EFTA citizens in specific situations (for example, after the first year of residence or for study reasons), and family members of permit B holders joining the holder in Swiss territory. ## # Residence Permit Requirements B
The B permit in the Obvaldo Canton follows federal criteria established by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), although the cantonal authority retains discretion in evaluating each application. The main requirements are:
1. ** Legitimate employment contract **: The foreigner must have an offer of employment confirmed by a Swiss employer. item.title: Wages and labour market Canton of Switzerland: sectors and levels
item.description: The labour market in the Canton of Schwyz: wage structure by degree of training, collective agreements, compulsory contributions and minimum rights.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - No federal minimum wage; some cantons set one by law - Wages vary by level of education (VET diploma, federal diploma, university degree) - OASI/IV contributions: 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - Collective labor agreements define pay standards by sector
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss wage structure by level of education and sector - OASI/IV contributions: 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - UI/ALV contributions: 1.1% up to an annual ceiling - Occupational pension (LPP/BVG): 7–18% according to age bracket (25–54+) - Health insurance (LAMal/KVG): mandatory for residents, per-capita premiums, not a payroll tax - Maximum working hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices) or 50 hours in other sectors
The labor market in the Canton of Schwyz follows the Swiss occupational structure, where wages are determined mainly by level of education, experience and sectoral collective agreements. Unlike many European countries, Switzerland does not set a federal minimum wage. Some cantons establish their own minimum wages through legislation, while others rely on sectoral collective agreements and market dynamics.
Education is the main driver of wage differentiation. Those who complete a vocational education and training (VET diploma of 3–4 years) gain access to technical and craft qualifications with higher pay than unskilled work. Those who obtain an advanced vocational diploma (federal diploma or federal examination) or a university degree access managerial and specialist roles with higher salaries.
### The contributions system on wages
In the Swiss pay system, the employee pays 5.3% of gross salary for OASI/IV (old-age and survivors' insurance and invalidity insurance) and EO/APG (loss-of-earnings compensation for maternity); the employer pays the matching 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. UI/ALV contributions (unemployment insurance) amount to 1.1% up to an annual ceiling. Accident insurance (UVG/LAA) ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the occupational sector. In addition, occupational pension provision (LPP/BVG) is mandatory for employees whose coordinated salary exceeds a threshold; contribution rates vary by age bracket: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ up to reference retirement age).
[Health insurance (LAMal/KVG)](nav:health) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and must be taken out within 3 months from the start of employment. It is not a payroll tax, but a private contract with per-capita premiums that vary by canton and region. Adults can choose annual deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500; higher premiums correspond to lower deductibles. ### Salary levels, training and collective contracts
The level of education remains the main differentiating factor in the Swiss labour market. Those who complete a vocational training (AFC) access typically higher salaries compared to unskilled work, with margins varying according to specialisation and market demand. Those who continue with higher education (federal diploma, federal examination, degree) access positions with greater responsibility and proportionally higher compensation.
Sectoral collective contracts (also called CCL or sectoral agreements) define minimum standards for salary, working hours and benefits for specific sectors: metallurgy, construction, commerce, pharmaceutical industry, advanced tertiary sector, and others. Even where there is no statutory cantonal minimum wage, collective contracts serve as an occupational reference and protect workers from compensation below certain levels.
### Working hours, holidays and minimum rights
Swiss law sets a maximum working time of 45 hours per week for industry, offices and sales; 50 hours for other sectors. Minimum holidays are 4 weeks per year (5 for those under 20). Maternity covers 14 weeks at 80% through loss-of-earnings compensation (IPG); paternity is 2 weeks. Notice periods for termination are: 1 month during the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards.
### Tax structure and pension provision
The Swiss tax system is structured on three levels: direct federal tax (IFD, uniform across the territory), cantonal taxes (varying by canton), and municipal taxes (applied as a multiplier on the cantonal rate). Canton Schwyz, like every canton, has its own cantonal tax rates and municipalities apply a local multiplier. The [occupational pension provision (LPP)](nav:pension) and the third pillar allow tax deductions for voluntary contributions, referring to federal and cantonal ordinances for details.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to navigate the Swiss labour market
For those seeking employment or negotiating a contract in Canton Schwyz, understanding how gross salary translates into net pay is essential. Many candidates do not correctly calculate the impact of mandatory insurance contributions on their actual take-home salary.
### Assessing gross salary and converting it to net
The first step is to gather salary benchmark data for your role, sector, and level of experience. If the employer adheres to a collective agreement, salaries are typically indexed to that scale. Online, bodies such as the FSO (Federal Statistical Office) and SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) publish median salary surveys by sector and canton.
Once you have identified a salary offer, it is essential to calculate the net amount: from gross salary you subtract AVS/AI contributions (5.3%), UI/ALV (1.1%), LAINF (0.7-1.5%), LPP (7-18% depending on age), and finally income taxes (federal, cantonal, municipal). A [salary calculator](nav:calculator) helps you visualise the net amount from a specific gross figure, including all contributions and taxes applicable in the canton.
### Choosing health insurance and reviewing the contract
Within 3 months of starting employment, the employee must take out a LAMal/KVG policy. Premiums vary significantly by canton and age bracket; choosing a higher deductible (up to CHF 2,500) reduces the monthly premium. Canton Schwyz offers premium subsidies for low-income earners, according to cantonal ordinances.
If the employer adheres to a collective agreement, request a copy of the applicable CLA (collective labour agreement), which specifies working hours, minimum wages, additional holidays, and benefits. If the proposed salary is below the collective agreement minimum, you have grounds to negotiate.
### Resources and next steps
To [search for specific job opportunities](nav:jobs) in the Swiss market, national platforms aggregate listings by sector and canton. Always calculate the net from the gross based on your personal and cantonal parameters using our [salary calculator](nav:calculator).

## Key facts - **What**: Registration in the Commercial Register in the Canton of Schwyz - When: Before the start of business - Where: Office of the Registrar of Commerce of the Canton of Schwyz - Who: Entrepreneurs, sole proprietorships, companies - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship, Sagl, SA - Minimum capital Sagl: CHF 20,000 - SA Minimum Capital: CHF 100,000 - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 10.6% total (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer)
The Canton of Swabia, like all Swiss cantons, requires compulsory registration in the Commercial Register for anyone intending to start a business. This procedure is the first administrative step and represents a crucial moment in the startup phase of any company. Before starting business operations, entrepreneurs and company owners must complete registration with the competent cantonal office, which varies depending on the legal form chosen.
The choice of legal form is decisive not only for organisational aspects, but also for financial and tax burdens. In the canton of Switzerland, as in the whole of Switzerland, there are several options: from the sole proprietorship (self-management) to the ### Three-tier tax system
In the Canton of Schwyz, as throughout Switzerland, the tax system operates on three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Each level has its own legislation and tax rate.
Direct Federal Tax (DFD) is administered by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA) and represents the federal level. Cantonal tax is managed by the cantonal authorities of Schwyz and is calculated according to its own cantonal law. Finally, municipalities apply a multiplier to the cantonal base, which means that local taxation varies depending on the company's domicile.
This three-tier structure requires the entrepreneur to consider not only the federal rate, but also the specific cantonal and municipal rates. This configuration is not found in many countries, where the tax system is centralized at one or two levels. To plan tax aspects, consult the federal tax calculator.
### Insurance obligations for employees
If the business involves hiring employees, significant insurance obligations arise immediately. Under Swiss labor law, the employer is required to pay social contributions for each employee.
⚠️ OASI (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance), DI (Disability Insurance), and EO (Income Compensation Allowance) contributions represent 5.3% of the employee's salary, to which an identical contribution from the employer is added, for a total of 10.6%. These contributions finance the first pillar of the Swiss pension system.
Accident insurance (UVG/LAA) is mandatory for employees working on a primary basis and varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity. This amount is borne by the employer.
For employees with an income of CHF 22,050 and above, the employer must also make payments for the second pension pillar (BVG/LPP), with rates that vary according to age: 7% between 25 and 34 years, 10% between 35 and 44 years, 15% between 45 and 54 years, and 18% from 55 years of age up to the reference age. To learn more about the second pillar, consult the [OASI/BVG guide](nav:pension).
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and must be taken out within 3 months of arrival. For employees, the cost depends on the cantonal premium (which varies by canton and region) and does not represent a direct cost for the employer, but is borne by the employee.
These charges represent a significant cost item in personnel management and must be considered in the startup budget. Their correct management is crucial for the success of the business.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure
To start a business in the Canton of Schwyz, following these steps is essential:
**1. Choose the legal form** Before taking any other action, define the type of enterprise. Consult an accountant or a lawyer specialized in commercial law to choose the structure that best suits your needs. Remember that the minimum capital varies: zero for sole proprietorships, CHF 20,000 for LLCs (Sagl), CHF 100,000 for corporations (SA).
2. Prepare the documentation Depending on the legal form, gather the necessary documents: Commercial Register extracts from previous experiences, identity documents of the owners, company statutes (for corporations), deed of incorporation, and bank certificates of capital deposit (for LLCs and SAs).
3. Register with the cantonal Commercial Register Contact the Commercial Register office of the Canton of Schwyz with the prepared documentation. Registration takes place at the competent cantonal authority and marks the official start of business activity.
4. Apply for the federal VAT number If the expected annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000, you must register for VAT with the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV). This number is necessary to issue invoices and manage federal tax obligations.
5. Register for cantonal and municipal taxes Contact the tax office of the Canton of Schwyz to register for cantonal and municipal taxes. You will receive details on deadlines, rates, and specific payment procedures.
6. Start social security contributions If you will be hiring employees, register with the competent OASI (AVS) Compensation Fund for the payment of social security contributions. Contact an insurance company for mandatory accident insurance.
7. Take out health insurance for employees Remember that every employee must have mandatory health insurance within 3 months of the start date. This is not the employer's direct duty, but ensure that your employees are covered.
### Important deadlines
Commercial Register registration must take place before the start of business. VAT registration, if necessary, has deadlines defined by the FTA. Social security contributions must begin from the month the first employee is hired. Annual tax returns have federal and cantonal deadlines that vary — your accountant will guide you on these.

3. Draft the founding deed and articles of association. For GmbH/Sàrl and AG/SA a public deed is required; for partnerships, a written contract between the partners may suffice.
4. Pay in the minimum capital and open a bank account. The payment must be certified by the bank and the amount deposited in the business account.
5. Register with the commercial register. The application is submitted to the cantonal office, with all required documents. The source notes the existence of registration fees, but the specific amount is not indicated: to be requested directly from the office.
6. Register with the tax authorities. Distinguish between direct federal tax/VAT (FTA/ESTV) and cantonal/municipal taxes (tax administration of Canton Schwyz). The source clarifies the respective competences: the FTA/ESTV handles direct federal tax and VAT, cantonal administrations handle the rest.
7. Register with a compensation fund. For OASI/DI/IC contributions and, if you hire employees, also unemployment insurance and LAINF (occupational accident insurance).
8. Take out the mandatory insurances. LAMal (health insurance) within 3 months of starting the activity for the owner and family members; LAINF for employees.
### Deadlines and recurring obligations
- VAT return: usually quarterly, with rates defined by the FTA. - Tax return: annual, with cantonal deadlines. - Payment of social security contributions: monthly or quarterly depending on the compensation fund.

To simulate the tax and social security impact on income, the Frontaliere Ticino [salary calculator](nav:calculator) is available. To compare the cost of living between cantons, also with a view to choosing where to locate the business, see the page on [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living). For those considering complementary pension solutions, the [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) offers an up-to-date overview.
Planning the start-up is a strategic phase: capital, legal form, tax regime and insurance coverage must be decided before registration, not after. Anticipating these steps reduces bureaucratic times and the risk of unexpected costs.

item.title: Buying a Svitto home: prices and mortgage
item.description: Practical guide: acquiring a property in the canton of Schwyz requires own funds, a sustainable mortgage, a transfer tax and notary fees. Complete procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Purchasing a home in the canton of Schwyz requires own funds and a sustainable mortgage. - The property transfer tax is a cantonal levy applied to real estate transactions. - Notary fees and registration in the land register are additional components of the total cost.
## Key facts
- **What**: Purchase of a home in the canton of Schwyz with assessment of prices, mortgage, own funds and taxes. - When: Procedure ranging from a few months (search) to a few weeks after the offer. - Where: Canton of Schwyz (Central Switzerland). - Who: Prospective buyers (residents, investors, foreigners with permits). - Amount: Variable depending on the property price, cantonal property transfer tax rate, and notary fees.
Those who decide to buy a house in the canton of Schwyz face an articulated procedure that touches on numerous aspects: from the assessment of market prices to the gathering of own funds, from the sustainability of the mortgage to the calculation of taxes and notary fees. The Canton of Schwyz, like every Swiss canton, applies its own tax rules and regulations that influence the final cost of the investment.
Purchasing a property is a significant financial decision, not only for the purchase price, but also for the initial capital outlay (own funds), the annual expenses (mortgage instalment, property taxes, insurance) and the one-off costs linked to the transfer of ownership (property transfer tax, notary fees, land register registration).
### Determining factors in the Schwyz real estate market
The value of properties in the Canton of Schwyz varies according to concrete factors: geographical location (proximity to main municipalities, accessibility by public transport), property characteristics (size, year of construction, state of maintenance) and the local economic context. At national level, the Swiss real estate market is monitored by federal statistical offices (FSO/BFS) and cantonal administrations, which publish periodic data on price trends.
You can consult the data on the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) to assess the overall sustainability of the property investment within the Swiss economic context. The mortgage is the fundamental tool for financing the purchase: Swiss banks offer tailored solutions, but they require solid guarantees in terms of own funds paid directly by the borrower. The sustainability of the monthly instalment is assessed by each institution according to shared federal criteria, with a prudential view of risk.
### The role of the mortgage in the transaction
The mortgage is not only a financing tool, but it directly affects the sustainability of the investment in the medium and long term. Banks require the borrower to demonstrate sufficient repayment capacity and to pay part of the price as own funds. This structure balances the risk between the lending institution and the buyer, protecting them from insolvency scenarios or fluctuations in the real estate market. ### Mortgage sustainability: criteria and assessment
Once the property has been identified and the purchase price defined, the next step is to verify whether the proposed mortgage is actually sustainable over time. Swiss banks apply strict criteria: the monthly instalment (principal + interest + insurance) must not exceed 30-35% of the household's gross monthly income. This ratio is called the 'debt-to-income ratio' (DTI) and varies slightly from one institution to another, but follows a logic of federal prudential soundness.
Even more cautious is the practice of the 'stress test': banks simulate a future scenario in which the interest rate rises by one or two percentage points compared to the current rate and verify that the instalment remains sustainable. If a scenario with higher rates were to make the instalment unsustainable, the mortgage amount is reduced. This mechanism protects the borrower in the event of future rate increases.
In addition to the main income, banks assess other financial obligations of the borrower: credit cards with active balances, car leases, personal loans. If the borrower has substantial payment obligations, the available mortgage capacity decreases. This integrated view of the credit profile reduces the risk of insolvency over time.
### Own funds: percentages and accumulation strategies
Swiss banks do not finance 100% of the purchase price. As a rule, the borrower must contribute at least 20% as own funds. This percentage acts as a safeguard: if the property value drops and the borrower can no longer repay the mortgage, the bank retains a margin of security in the value of the property.
Some institutions accept lower own funds (from 10% to 15%), but in that case they often require a mortgage credit insurance (LLM insurance) which the borrower must pay, increasing the total cost of the financing. Accumulating own funds takes time: many buyers build them up through private savings, inheritances, the sale of previous properties, or pension contributions (for example, a partial withdrawal from a private pension account [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3), where permitted by federal law and the institution's rules).
### Comparative scenarios: 70% vs. 80% vs. 90% mortgage
To illustrate the impact of own funds on sustainability, let's consider three hypothetical scenarios where the price is fixed, but the percentage of own funds varies. With the same interest rate and borrower's income, a mortgage financing 90% of the value (10% own funds) is more burdensome in terms of monthly instalment and carries the risk of additional insurance. A mortgage at 70-80% (20-30% own funds) reduces the monthly instalment and often does not require insurance, making the investment more sustainable in the medium to long term. This flexibility allows the borrower to tailor the financing to their own risk profile and financial resources.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure: from interest to the purchase deed
Step 1: Research and preliminary evaluation. The first step is to identify properties of interest in the Canton of Schwyz and request a preliminary assessment from banks or wealth managers. At this stage, the potential buyer provides information on income, assets, and available equity. The bank provides a (non-binding) indication of the mortgage amount that could be granted.
**Step 2: Offer and negotiation.** Once the desired property has been found, the buyer submits an offer to the seller. Negotiations may concern the price, handover date, and maintenance work. During this phase, it is advisable to request a formal property valuation from a bank appraiser.
Step 3: Formal mortgage application. Once the offer is defined, the borrower submits a formal mortgage application to the bank, attaching documentation: bank statements, tax returns, the offer letter, and the property valuation. The bank carries out a detailed credit analysis and communicates the amount it can grant and the terms (rate, duration, monthly instalment).
Step 4: Notary and deed of sale. Once the mortgage is confirmed, the parties turn to a notary. In the Canton of Schwyz, the notary draws up the deed of sale (rogito), which must comply with the formalities required by cantonal law. The deed describes the property, the contracting parties, the price, the conditions of transfer, and the incidence of the transfer tax.
Step 5: Disbursement of funds and registration. Before the final signature, the borrower pays in the agreed equity. At the same time, the bank subscribes the mortgage loan and registers it with the cantonal land registry (Grundbuch), obtaining a mortgage lien on the property. The entry in the land registry is managed by the competent office of the Canton of Schwyz.
Step 6: Transfer of ownership. Upon signing of the notarial deed, ownership is transferred from the seller to the buyer. The transfer tax is calculated and paid according to the procedures set out by Swiss cantonal law.
### Transfer tax and notary fees: components of the final cost
The transfer tax is a cantonal levy that applies to the transfer of ownership of a property. Each Swiss canton sets its own rates and rules: the Canton of Schwyz, like other central cantons, applies this tax according to specific laws and regulations. The amount depends on the value of the property at the time of transfer. Exemptions are often provided for transfers between spouses, direct descendants, or ascendants; the exact conditions vary by canton and require verification with the notary.
Notary fees cover the drafting of the deed, authentication, and the administrative handling of the sale. These fees are set by cantonal tariffs and typically amount to 1–2% of the property value, depending on the complexity of the transaction.
Additional costs include the registration in the land registry (cantonal office fees) and any costs for an appraiser or real estate agency. Together, these additional charges usually amount to 3–5% of the purchase price.
